summary: Discusses how a company's data classification policy can be mapped onto the S/MIME security label. It gives worked examples drawn from the policies of three real companies.

plainLanguage.summary: A company marks its documents by how sensitive they are, and that mark has to travel inside the signed email if the recipient's system is to act on it. This memo shows how three real company policies could be written into the security label defined for S/MIME, and how a recipient's permission to read a given label is carried alongside their certificate.

questions: map company classification policy to s/mime
how do companies control who can read classified email
what is an s/mime security label
how do i implement company security policy in email
subtitle: How to mark signed email with a company's own classification levels, so a recipient's system can act on them.

tldr.problem: A company classifies its information, but the classification has to travel inside the signed message for a recipient's mail system to enforce anything.
tldr.mechanism: The memo shows how three real classification policies are mapped onto the ESSSecurityLabel defined in RFC 2634, using a policy identifier, a hierarchical classification, an optional privacy mark and optional security categories, and shows how the recipient's clearance is carried in an attribute certificate.
tldr.outcome: The examples use test object identifiers rather than real ones, so the memo is Informational and adds no protocol of its own. All the security considerations of RFC 2630 and RFC 2634 apply.

today: RFC 3114 is an Informational memo, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It works out examples from the classification policies in force at Amoco, Caterpillar and Whirlpool at the time of writing, and the object identifiers it defines are test identifiers rather than real ones. It is read with RFC 2634, which defines the security label syntax, and RFC 3281, the attribute certificate profile it uses for clearances.

sections.title: Security Labels and Company Policy
sections.content:
Security labels are an optional security service for S/MIME. A security label is a set of security information about the sensitivity of the content that is protected by the S/MIME encapsulation. A security label can be included in the signed attributes of any SignedData object, and a security label attribute may be included in the inner signature, the outer signature, or both. The syntax and processing rules for security labels are described in RFC 2634.

The memo discusses how company security policy for data classification maps onto that label, using policies that were in force at three companies as worked examples.

The background is that information is an asset, but not all information has the same value for a business. Research and development plans, marketing strategies and manufacturing quality specifications give a company competitive advantage, and this kind of information needs stronger protective measures than other information which, if disclosed or modified, would cause moderate to severe damage. Other material, such as internal organisation charts, employee lists and policies, may need little or no protective measures based on the value the organisation places on it. A corporate information classification policy defines how its information assets are to be protected, provides guidance to employees on how to classify them, and defines how to label and protect an asset based on its classification and its state, for example a facsimile, an electronic transfer, storage or shipping.
sections.plainLanguage: The security label is a place inside a signed message where the sender can say how sensitive the content is. The memo's job is to show how a company would write its own classification scheme into that label, so that the receiving system can read it and act on it.

sections.title: Access Control and Security Labels
sections.content:
Access control is a means of enforcing authorizations, and several styles of it exist. Rule based access control uses policies that can be algorithmically expressed. Identity based access control applies a policy explicitly to an individual person or host entity, or to a defined group of such entities, and grants access once the identity has been authenticated and verified to be on the access list. Rank based access control is based on hierarchical positions in an organisation, so a policy would define what information the position of Partner or Senior Consultant could access. Role based access control is based on roles in the organisation, whether or not those roles are hierarchical, so a policy would define what information the role of Database Administrator, Network Administrator, Mailroom Clerk or Purchaser could access.

Rule, rank and role based access control can rely on a security label as the security mechanism that conveys the sensitivity or classification of the information. When an S/MIME encapsulated message is processed, the sensitivity information in the message's security label can be compared with the recipient's authorizations to determine whether the recipient is allowed to access the protected content.

A label may sit in the inner signature, the outer signature, or both. In the case of a triple-wrapped message as defined in RFC 2634, the inner signature would be used for access control decisions related to the plaintext original content, while the outer signature would be used for decisions related to the encrypted message.

Users also need to be granted authorizations to access information that has been classified by an authority, and the sending and receiving agents need to be able to determine those authorizations securely. X.509 and the Internet profile for X.509 certificates do not define the means to represent and convey authorizations in a certificate. X.501 does, in the form of a clearance attribute, which identifies the security policy in force to which a list of possible classifications and security categories relates, and X.501 also notes two means for binding the clearance to a named entity: an Attribute Certificate, and a certificate extension field, for example one within the subjectDirectoryAttribute extension. RFC 3281 defines a profile of X.509 Attribute Certificate suitable for use with authorization information within Internet protocols, and one of the attributes it defines is Clearance, which carries clearance information about the owner of the attribute certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: There are several ways to decide who may read what. The label is the part that travels with the message; the clearance is the part that says what a particular person is allowed to read, and it is carried in a separate certificate.

sections.title: Mapping a Policy onto the Security Label
sections.content:
The examples build on the ESSSecurityLabel syntax and processing rules of RFC 2634 and use its components in turn.

The security policy identifier names the security policy in force to which the label relates, and so indicates the semantics of the other components. The memo defines a set of test policy object identifiers under the S/MIME working group registry: id-smime is the arc iso(1) member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549) pkcs(1) pkcs-9(9) 16, the test security policy arc id-tsp is id-smime 7, and the three test policies are id-tsp-TEST-Amoco, id-tsp-TEST-Caterpillar and id-tsp-TEST-Whirlpool.

The security classification values and their meanings are defined by the governing company policies, and the values defined are hierarchical and do not use the integers 0 through 5. Amoco defines amoco-general as 6, amoco-confidential as 7 and amoco-highly-confidential as 8. Caterpillar defines caterpillar-public as 6, caterpillar-green as 7, caterpillar-yellow as 8 and caterpillar-red as 9. Whirlpool defines whirlpool-public as 6, whirlpool-internal as 7 and whirlpool-confidential as 8.

Privacy marks are specified in the Whirlpool policy, which gives examples of possible markings, with others left for users to define. The examples are MAKE NO COPIES, THIRD PARTY CONFIDENTIAL, ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGED DOCUMENT, DISTRIBUTION LIMITED TO, and COVERED BY A NON-ANALYSIS AGREEMENT. The Amoco policy identifies no privacy marks, but the memo notes that its availability and integrity labels would be most appropriately displayed there, and that the CRITICAL, MAXIMUM, MEDIUM and MINIMUM labels are examples of information classifications that are not used for access control. In general the privacy marks should give brief but clear direction to the user on how to handle the information.

Security categories, or caveats, are not specified in any of the sample policies, although they are used in at least two of the companies. Once locally defined they are formal and are to be enforced, and they are defined when necessary to provide identifiable proprietary information more granular access control. A category can be based organizationally or by project, for example Legal Only or Project Vallor. They are represented in the RFC 2634 ESSSecurityLabel, which specifies the sensitivity of labeled data, and in the X.501 Clearance attribute, which specifies an entity's authorizations, using a set of security categories with a bound of 64. Each category is a sequence of a type, itself an object identifier, and a value defined by that type. One example syntax, named SecurityCategoryValues, uses a sequence of UTF8 strings as the value. An organisation defines its own category type object identifier, and access MUST be restricted to only those entities who are authorized to access every category value on the label. Access is authorized if the category value in the label EXACTLY matches the category value in the clearance.
sections.plainLanguage: Each label names the policy it belongs to, carries a number for the classification level, may carry a short note about how to handle the content, and may carry extra tags that narrow who may see it. The numbers are chosen by each company, starting at 6 rather than 0.

sections.title: A Worked Label and Clearance
sections.content:
The memo works through one example in full. It uses the Whirlpool test policy and assumes that the security policy identified by id-tsp-TEST-Whirlpool defines one security category type object identifier, id-tsp-TEST-Whirlpool-Categories, whose value is id-tsp 4.

The example ESSSecurityLabel has the security policy identifier id-tsp-3, a security classification of 8, the privacy mark ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGED INFORMATION, and one security category whose type is id-tsp-4 and whose value is LAW DEPARTMENT USE ONLY.

Two example clearance attributes are given. The first passes the access control check: its policy identifier is id-tsp-3, its class list sets bits 6, 7 and 8 to TRUE, and its security category has type id-tsp-4 and value LAW DEPARTMENT USE ONLY, so it matches the label exactly. The second fails the check because the category values do not match: its class list also sets bits 6, 7 and 8 to TRUE, but its category value is HUMAN RESOURCES USE ONLY.

The clearance attributes for the three companies follow the same pattern, each carrying the policy identifier of its own test policy and a class list. The Amoco user lists amoco-general, amoco-confidential and amoco-highly-confidential as 6, 7 and 8. The Caterpillar user lists caterpillar-public, caterpillar-confidential-green, caterpillar-confidential-yellow and caterpillar-confidential-red as 6, 7, 8 and 9. The Whirlpool user lists whirlpool-public, whirlpool-internal and whirlpool-confidential as 6, 7 and 8.
sections.plainLanguage: The example label says the document is at level 8, is privileged material for the law department, and may only be seen by someone cleared for exactly that. One clearance matches and passes; another, holding a different category, fails.

sections.title: Two Implementation Issues
sections.content:
One implementation issue is the mapping of the security label values to displayable characters. This matters for users who want to develop and retire their own classifications and categories on a regular basis, and when the values are encoded in non-human readable form. Applications should provide a means for the enterprise to manage these changes, and the practice of hard coding the mapping into the applications is discouraged. The memo views this as a local issue for the application vendor, because the solution does not need to be interoperable between vendors. One approach is the use of a Security Policy Information File, a construct that conveys domain-specific security policy information. A SPIF is a signed object, to protect it from unauthorized changes and to authenticate the source of the policy information. It contains critical display information, such as the text string for security classifications and security categories to be displayed to the user, as well as additional security policy information.

The other implementation issue is obtaining the recipient's certificate when sending a signed-only message with a security label. Normally the recipient's certificate is only needed when sending an encrypted message, but applications need to be able to retrieve the recipient's certificate so that the recipient's clearance information is available for the access control check.
sections.plainLanguage: Two practical problems. The numbers in the label have to be turned into words people can read, and that mapping should live in one managed place rather than be hard coded. And the sender needs the recipient's certificate even for a signed-only message, because the clearance is inside it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: All the security considerations from RFC 2630 and RFC 2634 apply to applications that use the procedures described in the memo. There are no further ones, because the memo adds no protocol behaviour of its own: it shows how an existing security label and an existing clearance attribute can carry a company's own classification policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds nothing to the security rules that already apply to signed and encrypted mail; it only fills in the fields of a label that already exists.

viz.caption: THE FOUR STYLES OF ACCESS CONTROL THE MEMO DESCRIBES

items.title: Rule based
items.text: The policy can be expressed as rules that a machine can evaluate.

items.title: Identity based
items.text: The policy names a person, a host or a group, and access follows an access list.

items.title: Rank based
items.text: The policy follows the person's position in the company structure.

items.title: Role based
items.text: The policy follows the job the person does, whether or not the roles are ranked.

viz.caption: THE CLASSIFICATION VALUES OF THE THREE EXAMPLE POLICIES

cells: Separate integrity levels MAXIMUM, MEDIUM and MINIMUM, and an availability level CRITICAL
None in the policy as quoted
Privacy marks such as MAKE NO COPIES

viz.caption: THE EXAMPLE LABEL AND A CLEARANCE THAT PASSES THE CHECK

data.title: ESSSecurityLabel and Clearance
data.code:
Example ESSSecurityLabel:
 security-policy-identifier: id-tsp-3
 security-classification: 8
 privacy-mark: ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGED INFORMATION
 security-categories: SEQUENCE OF SecurityCategory

SecurityCategory #1
  type:  id-tsp-4
  value:  LAW DEPARTMENT USE ONLY

Example Clearance Attribute #1 (passes access control check):

Clearance:
 policyId: id-tsp-3
 classList BIT STRING: Bits 6, 7, 8 are set to TRUE
 securityCategories: SEQUENCE OF SecurityCategory

SecurityCategory #1
  type:  id-tsp-4
  value:  LAW DEPARTMENT USE ONLY
